sentences.text: The genus name Mantellisaurus honors Gideon Mantell, the discoverer of Iguanodon. This lightly constructed iguanodontian dinosaur reached a length of 7 meters and a weight of 750 kilograms. It was smaller than Iguanodon bernissartensis, with an estimated weight of 750 kg. The forelimbs of Mantellisaurus were proportionally shorter than those of Iguanodon bernissartensis.
Mantellisaurus was smaller than Iguanodon bernissartensis, with an estimated weight of 750 kg. It reached a length of 7 meters and a weight of 750 kilograms.

The holotype specimen was discovered by Reginald Walter Hooley in 1914 in southern England and reported in 1917. Reginald Walter Hooley named the species Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925, after his death. The species name 'atherfieldensis' refers to the village of Atherfield on the Isle of Wight where the fossil was found. The holotype fossils of Mantellisaurus were discovered in 1917 by Reginald Hooley in Atherfield on the Isle of Wight, England. Reginald Hooley named the species Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925, after his death.

A significant specimen was discovered in a quarry in Maidstone, Kent, in February 1834. Gideon Mantell purchased the Maidstone specimen for £25 in June 1834. Gideon Mantell identified the Maidstone specimen as an Iguanodon based on its distinctive teeth. Mantell incorrectly placed a horn on the nose of the Iguanodon reconstruction based on this specimen.
Fossil remains of Mantellisaurus have been found in Belgium, England, Spain, and Germany. The genus contains only one species, Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis.

Specimen IRSNB 1551 became the second mounted non-avian dinosaur skeleton made primarily of actual bone when displayed by Louis Dollo in 1884. This Belgian specimen was originally assigned to Iguanodon mantelli in 1881 but was later thought to belong to Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1986. Gregory S. Paul assigned this specimen to the genus and species Dollodon bampingi in 2008. In 2010, Kenneth Carpenter and Yusuke Ishida synonymized Dollodon bampingi with Iguanodon seelyi.

In 1971, a quarry near Nehden, Germany, yielded numerous disarticulated iguanodontid remains, mostly Mantellisaurus, alongside other dinosaur and crocodylian fragments. Mantellisaurus fossils are known from several localities in Spain, including an articulated hindlimb from Las Hoyas and a specimen from Rubielos de Mora. Three Mantellisaurus specimens are known from the Arcillas de Morella Formation in Spain.

Gregory Paul proposed that Mantellisaurus was primarily bipedal, using all fours only when standing still or moving slowly. Gregory S. Paul proposed that Mantellisaurus was primarily bipedal, using four legs only when standing or moving slowly.
Gregory Paul established the genus Mantellisaurus in 2007, separating it from Iguanodon atherfieldensis. Gregory S. Paul recognized Mantellisaurus as a distinct dinosaur genus in 2006.

A 2010 cladistic analysis by McDonald, Barrett, and Chapman suggested that Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis is a sister taxon to Dollodon bampingi. Both Mantellisaurus and Dollodon are considered the most basal representatives of the clade Hadrosauroidea, which includes hadrosaurids and taxa more closely related to them than to Iguanodon.

Mantellisaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the early Aptian ages. This iguanodontian dinosaur lived in Europe during the Barremian and early Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous. Mantellisaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago, between the Barremian and Aptian stages in what is now Europe.

The validity of the genus Dollodon is disputed among researchers. In 2012, Andrew McDonald considered Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis to be a synonym of Dollodon bampingi and possibly Proplanicoxa galtoni. The validity of the genus Dollodon has been disputed since its description.
